prompt: Ultra-close-up top-down photograph of an antique entomology specimen drawer, museum archival lighting. Deep charcoal velvet pinning substrate with visible fabric texture and slight wear. Dark walnut wood visible only at the very edges of the frame. On the left quarter of the image, approximately 20 to 25 pinned butterfly and moth specimens are vivid, three-dimensional, and intact — each genuinely unique in species, size, wingspan, and pin angle, ranging from a large iridescent blue morpho to a tiny cream-winged skipper, wings showing microscopic scale detail and natural asymmetry, bodies casting soft shallow shadows on the velvet. Moving right, the specimens progressively deteriorate in an organic, uneven wave rather than a clean line — some columns fade faster than others, creating a ragged frontier of disappearance. By the center of the frame, specimens are translucent grey impressions. By two-thirds across, only powder residue and tarnished pin heads remain in the velvet. The rightmost third of the frame is almost entirely empty velvet, with scattered lonely pins and faint chalk-dust outlines where wings once pressed — this emptiness fills the frame edge to edge with no blank padding. The overall ratio of vivid to absent is roughly one to three, so emptiness dominates the image. Warm single-source spotlight from upper left. No text. No border. No labels. Photorealistic Hasselblad macro photography, extreme depth of field, dust particles faintly visible in the light
dataset_name: Twenty years (2000-2020) of butterfly monitoring data across the contiguous United States
insight: Across 35 U.S. monitoring programs, butterfly abundance fell by 22% between 2000 and 2020.
